claim: Enhanced expression of the MYC transcription factor is observed in the majority of tumors.
source: Enhanced expression of the MYC transcription factor is observed in the majority of tumors.
evidence: Supported by citations to Dang, 2012 and Meyer and Penn, 2008 in the introduction.

claim: Deregulated expression of one of the three members of the MYC gene family (MYC, MYCN or MYCL) is observed in the majority of human tumors.
source: Deregulated expression of one of the three members of the MYC gene family (MYC, MYCN or MYCL) is observed in the majority of human tumors (Dang, 2012; Meyer and Penn, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Dang, 2012; Meyer and Penn, 2008).

claim: Deregulated MYC expression causally contributes to multiple aspects of tumor development.
source: A broad body of evidence establishes that deregulated MYC expression causally contributes to multiple aspects of tumor development and that tumors depend on enhanced expression of MYC for growth and survival (Casey et al., 2016; Soucek et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Casey et al., 2016 and Soucek et al., 2013.

claim: Tumors depend on enhanced expression of MYC for growth and survival.
source: A broad body of evidence establishes that deregulated MYC expression causally contributes to multiple aspects of tumor development and that tumors depend on enhanced expression of MYC for growth and survival (Casey et al., 2016; Soucek et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Casey et al., 2016 and Soucek et al., 2013.

claim: MYC proteins are transcription factors that bind DNA as part of several protein complexes.
source: MYC proteins are transcription factors that bind DNA as part of several protein complexes; best understood is a dimeric complex of MYC with its partner protein MAX that activates transcription via binding to a specific DNA motif termed E-box with a consensus sequence of CACGTG (Conacci-Sorrell et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Conacci-Sorrell et al., 2014.

claim: The MYC/MAX dimeric complex activates transcription via binding to E-box sequences with a consensus sequence of CACGTG.
source: best understood is a dimeric complex of MYC with its partner protein MAX that activates transcription via binding to a specific DNA motif termed E-box with a consensus sequence of CACGTG (Conacci-Sorrell et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Conacci-Sorrell et al., 2014.

claim: The binary MYC/MAX complex associates with MIZ1 to repress transcription.
source: To repress transcription, the binary MYC/MAX complex associates with a zinc finger protein termed MIZ1 (Wiese et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wiese et al., 2013.

claim: MYC is present on virtually all promoters with an open chromatin structure.
source: ChIP (chromatin-immunoprecipitation) (Fernandez et al., 2003) and ChIP-sequencing experiments (Lin et al., 2012; Nie et al., 2012; Sabò et al., 2014) demonstrate the presence of MYC on virtually all promoters with an open chromatin structure as well as on thousands of enhancers and intergenic sites in multiple cell types, raising the question what the functional relevance of this broad binding might be.
evidence: Supported by citations to ChIP and ChIP-sequencing experiments (Fernandez et al., 2003; Lin et al., 2012; Nie et al., 2012; Sabò et al., 2014).

claim: MYC is present on thousands of enhancers and intergenic sites in multiple cell types.
source: ChIP (chromatin-immunoprecipitation) (Fernandez et al., 2003) and ChIP-sequencing experiments (Lin et al., 2012; Nie et al., 2012; Sabò et al., 2014) demonstrate the presence of MYC on virtually all promoters with an open chromatin structure as well as on thousands of enhancers and intergenic sites in multiple cell types, raising the question what the functional relevance of this broad binding might be.
evidence: Supported by citations to ChIP-sequencing experiments (Lin et al., 2012; Nie et al., 2012; Sabò et al., 2014).

claim: MYC-driven tumors can be recognized by a specific set of up- and down-regulated MYC target genes.
source: Given this global binding pattern, it is surprising that MYC-driven tumors can be recognized by a specific set of up- and down-regulated MYC target genes that holds considerable prognostic and therapeutic value (Sabò et al., 2014; Walz et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sabò et al., 2014 and Walz et al., 2014.

claim: The general amplifier model proposes that MYC proteins globally enhance transcription.
source: One hypothesis to explain this observation suggests that MYC proteins globally enhance transcription. This has been termed the general amplifier model (Lin et al., 2012; Nie et al., 2012) and is supported by observations that MYC can cause an increase in total RNA and mRNA levels (Grandori et al., 2005; Hsu et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2012; Nie et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lin et al., 2012; Nie et al., 2012; Grandori et al., 2005; Hsu et al., 2015.

claim: MYC can cause an increase in total RNA and mRNA levels.
source: This has been termed the general amplifier model (Lin et al., 2012; Nie et al., 2012) and is supported by observations that MYC can cause an increase in total RNA and mRNA levels (Grandori et al., 2005; Hsu et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2012; Nie et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grandori et al., 2005; Hsu et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2012; Nie et al., 2012.

claim: The alternative model suggests that MYC proteins regulate specific genes.
source: The alternative viewpoint suggests that MYC proteins regulate specific genes and that global changes in RNA and mRNA levels occur indirectly as a consequence of MYC-driven cell growth (Sabò and Amati, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sabò and Amati, 2014.

claim: Global changes in RNA and mRNA levels occur indirectly as a consequence of MYC-driven cell growth.
source: The alternative viewpoint suggests that MYC proteins regulate specific genes and that global changes in RNA and mRNA levels occur indirectly as a consequence of MYC-driven cell growth (Sabò and Amati, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sabò and Amati, 2014.

claim: Much of MYC binding to chromatin is non-productive in terms of transcriptional regulation according to the specific gene regulation model.
source: To explain the contrast between global binding and specific gene regulation, the latter model proposes that much of MYC binding to chromatin is non-productive in terms of transcriptional regulation (Kress et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kress et al., 2015.

claim: U2OS cells express relatively low levels of endogenous MYC despite being tumor cells.
source: We chose U2OS cells because they have relatively low levels of endogenous MYC, despite being tumor cells.
evidence: Stated in the manuscript text and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1B.

claim: U2OS cells express levels of MYC that are comparable to non-transformed cells (IMEC, HMLE, MCF10A).
source: The results show that U2OS cells express levels of MYC that are comparable to non-transformed cells (IMEC, HMLE, MCF10A) and lower than those found in other tumor cell lines (HeLa and HCT116).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B comparing MYC levels across cell lines.

claim: U2OS cells express lower MYC levels than HeLa and HCT116 tumor cell lines.
source: The results show that U2OS cells express levels of MYC that are comparable to non-transformed cells (IMEC, HMLE, MCF10A) and lower than those found in other tumor cell lines (HeLa and HCT116).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Prolonged exposure (>3 days) to doxycycline induces apoptosis in U2OS cells.
source: Notably, prolonged exposure (>3 days) to doxycycline and hence long-term ectopic expression of MYC induces apoptosis in U2OS cells (Walz et al., 2014); therefore, all subsequent analyses were performed 28–30 hr after addition of doxycycline.
evidence: Supported by citation to Walz et al., 2014.

claim: Endogenous MYC binds to about 5,500 promoters in U2OS cells.
source: ChIP-sequencing of MYC in U2OSTet-on cells had previously shown that endogenous MYC binds to about 5,500 promoters and that this number increases to about 8,400 MYC-bound promoters upon addition of doxycycline (Walz et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous ChIP-sequencing data (Walz et al., 2014).

claim: MYC binding increases to about 8,400 promoters upon addition of doxycycline in U2OS cells.
source: ChIP-sequencing of MYC in U2OSTet-on cells had previously shown that endogenous MYC binds to about 5,500 promoters and that this number increases to about 8,400 MYC-bound promoters upon addition of doxycycline (Walz et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous ChIP-sequencing data (Walz et al., 2014).

claim: Individual promoters show a wide range of occupancies for endogenous MYC.
source: In agreement with reports from other systems, we concluded that the promoters of the majority of all expressed genes are bound by MYC. Surprisingly, individual promoters showed a wide range of occupancies for endogenous MYC (Figure 1C–E), whereas the differences in occupancy by MYC among promoters were much smaller after induction with doxycycline (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-sequencing data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: Differences in MYC occupancy among promoters are much smaller after induction with doxycycline.
source: Surprisingly, individual promoters showed a wide range of occupancies for endogenous MYC (Figure 1C–E), whereas the differences in occupancy by MYC among promoters were much smaller after induction with doxycycline (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-sequencing data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: Promoters most weakly bound by endogenous MYC recruit most MYC upon overexpression.
source: Promoters, which are least strongly bound by endogenous MYC recruit most MYC upon overexpression (i.e. VEGFA, Figure 1E), whereas the most strongly bound genes recruit no additional MYC (i.e. RPL8).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-sequencing data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The most strongly bound genes recruit no additional MYC upon overexpression.
source: Promoters, which are least strongly bound by endogenous MYC recruit most MYC upon overexpression (i.e. VEGFA, Figure 1E), whereas the most strongly bound genes recruit no additional MYC (i.e. RPL8).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-sequencing data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Genes most weakly bound by endogenous MYC (mean: 89 tags) recruit MYC most strongly (5.3-fold).
source: Strikingly, genes, which are most weakly bound (mean: 89 tags), recruit MYC most strongly (5.3-fold), whereas the most strongly bound genes (mean: 580 tags) show on average no further MYC recruitment.
evidence: Supported by binned plot analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The most strongly bound genes (mean: 580 tags) show on average no further MYC recruitment.
source: Strikingly, genes, which are most weakly bound (mean: 89 tags), recruit MYC most strongly (5.3-fold), whereas the most strongly bound genes (mean: 580 tags) show on average no further MYC recruitment.
evidence: Supported by binned plot analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Genes strongly bound by endogenous MYC levels are fully occupied ('saturated').
source: One way to explain this observation is the hypothesis that genes strongly bound by endogenous MYC levels are fully occupied ('saturated') and hence exogenous MYC is preferentially recruited to weakly bound genes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the observed data patterns.

claim: MYC/MAX heterodimers compete with MXD/MAX heterodimers and MAX homodimers for binding to their target sites.
source: To test whether this explanation is correct, we made use of the observation that MYC/MAX heterodimers compete with MXD/MAX heterodimers and MAX homodimers for binding to their target sites (Conacci-Sorrell et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Conacci-Sorrell et al., 2014.

claim: MXD6 occupancy is barely detectable above background for genes strongly occupied by endogenous MYC (NPM1, NCL).
source: Binding of MXD6 was barely detectable above background for the two genes (NPM1, NCL), which are strongly occupied by endogenous MYC, and did not further decrease upon addition of doxycycline.
evidence: Supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: MXD6 occupancy is higher for genes poorly bound by endogenous MYC (HSPBAP1, FBX32) and strongly decreases upon induction of MYC.
source: In contrast, MXD6 occupancy was higher for two genes (HSPBAP1, FBX32), which are poorly bound by endogenous MYC, but strongly decreased upon induction of MYC.
evidence: Supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: A few hundred promoters are saturated by endogenous MYC in U2OS cells.
source: Taken together, the easiest model to explain the data is to suggest that a few hundred of promoters are saturated by endogenous MYC in U2OS cells and that overexpression of MYC leads to saturation of the majority of MYC-binding sites in promoters (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Overexpression of MYC leads to saturation of the majority of MYC-binding sites in promoters.
source: Taken together, the easiest model to explain the data is to suggest that a few hundred of promoters are saturated by endogenous MYC in U2OS cells and that overexpression of MYC leads to saturation of the majority of MYC-binding sites in promoters (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: U2OS cells express approximately 100,000 molecules of endogenous MYC per cell.
source: From triplicate experiments, we estimated that U2OS cells express approximately 100,000 molecules of endogenous MYC per cell and that this number increases to approximately 3x106 molecules of MYC upon induction with 1 μg/ml doxycycline (see calculations in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunoblot data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: MYC levels increase to approximately 3x10^6 molecules per cell upon induction with 1 μg/ml doxycycline in U2OS cells.
source: From triplicate experiments, we estimated that U2OS cells express approximately 100,000 molecules of endogenous MYC per cell and that this number increases to approximately 3x106 molecules of MYC upon induction with 1 μg/ml doxycycline (see calculations in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunoblot data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: Two human tumor cell lines derived from small cell lung cancer and multiple myeloma express up to 880,000 molecules of MYC per cell.
source: Previous estimates found that two human tumor cell lines derived from small cell lung cancer and multiple myeloma express up to 880,000 molecules of MYC per cell (Lin et al., 2012), confirming that upon maximal induction with doxycycline most U2OS cells express MYC levels comparable or slightly higher to levels found in human tumor cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lin et al., 2012.

claim: Upon maximal induction with doxycycline, most U2OS cells express MYC levels comparable or slightly higher to levels found in human tumor cells.
source: Previous estimates found that two human tumor cell lines derived from small cell lung cancer and multiple myeloma express up to 880,000 molecules of MYC per cell (Lin et al., 2012), confirming that upon maximal induction with doxycycline most U2OS cells express MYC levels comparable or slightly higher to levels found in human tumor cells.
evidence: Based on comparison with published data (Lin et al., 2012) and the authors' own measurements.

claim: Endogenous MYC levels vary less than +/− 3.7-fold in 80% of all U2OS cells.
source: Staining and quantification with three different antibodies demonstrated that endogenous MYC levels vary less than +/− 3.7-fold in 80% of all cells (EtOH, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C) and less than +/− 2.9-fold upon overexpression (doxycycline, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: MYC levels vary less than +/− 2.9-fold in 80% of U2OS cells upon overexpression with doxycycline.
source: Staining and quantification with three different antibodies demonstrated that endogenous MYC levels vary less than +/− 3.7-fold in 80% of all cells (EtOH, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C) and less than +/− 2.9-fold upon overexpression (doxycycline, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: EC50 values of individual promoters vary over a large concentration range.
source: A density plot illustrates that EC50 values of individual promoters vary over a large concentration range (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by density plot shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Genes encoding ribosomal proteins show the lowest EC50 values.
source: Notably, genes encoding ribosomal proteins (RPs) showed the lowest EC50 values, followed by genes encoding proteins involved in biosynthetic processes, translation and ribosome biogenesis (Figure 2D; gene sets are shown in Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Genes encoding proteins involved in biosynthetic processes, translation and ribosome biogenesis show low EC50 values.
source: Notably, genes encoding ribosomal proteins (RPs) showed the lowest EC50 values, followed by genes encoding proteins involved in biosynthetic processes, translation and ribosome biogenesis (Figure 2D; gene sets are shown in Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Genes encoding metabolite transporters, G-protein coupled receptors and genes involved in TGF-beta signaling and response to hypoxia show the highest EC50 values.
source: At the other extreme, genes encoding metabolite transporters, G-protein coupled receptors and genes involved in TGF-beta signaling and in the response to hypoxia are among those with the highest EC50 values (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: MYC/MAX heterodimers bind to canonical E-boxes (CACGTG), non-canonical E-boxes (CANNTG) and DNA with a random sequence.
source: The heterodimer makes both base-specific contacts and contacts to the phosphate backbone of DNA and hence binds to canonical E-boxes (CACGTG), non-canonical E-boxes (CANNTG) and DNA with a random sequence (Nair and Burley, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nair and Burley, 2003.

claim: Only 363 of 8,425 promoters show an EC50 value of 1x10^2 μM or higher.
source: Under these assumptions, MYC/MAX complexes are predicted to bind canonical E-boxes with a calculated EC50 value of 1x102 μM (Figure 3D). Comparison with the experimentally determined EC50 values showed that only 363 of 8,425 promoters show this or a higher EC50 value.
evidence: Based on modeling results shown in Figure 3D compared with experimental data.

claim: Binding to DNA alone is not sufficient to account for the chromatin occupancy of MYC observed by ChIP-sequencing.
source: The majority of E-boxes located in promoters showed considerably lower EC50 values than those predicted by the affinity to E-box-DNA, indicating that binding to DNA alone is not sufficient to account for the chromatin occupancy of MYC observed by ChIP-sequencing.
evidence: Based on comparison of predicted and observed EC50 values.

claim: Occupancy by endogenous MYC positively correlates with the occurrence of canonical E-box sequences in the binding region.
source: Consistent with the DNA binding properties, we found a strong correlation between the occupancy of endogenous MYC and the occurrence of canonical E-box sequences in the binding region (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: Supported by binned plot analysis shown in Figure 4A and supplementary figures.

claim: Non-consensus E-box sequences are only moderately enriched in MYC peaks and their frequency does not positively correlate with MYC binding.
source: In contrast, non-consensus E-box sequences are only moderately enriched in MYC peaks and their frequency does not positively correlate with MYC binding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,D-F).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,D-F.

claim: Occupancy by endogenous MYC positively correlates with overall expression of the respective gene.
source: In addition to canonical E-box sequences in the binding region, occupancy by endogenous MYC positively correlated with overall expression of the respective gene (Figure 4B) and with features of open chromatin, such as trimethylation of histone H3K4 (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by binned plot analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Occupancy by endogenous MYC positively correlates with trimethylation of histone H3K4.
source: In addition to canonical E-box sequences in the binding region, occupancy by endogenous MYC positively correlated with overall expression of the respective gene (Figure 4B) and with features of open chromatin, such as trimethylation of histone H3K4 (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by binned plot analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: WDR5 is a direct interaction partner of MYC.
source: Recent work has identified WDR5, a WD40-repeat-containing protein, which is a part of the MLL/SET methyltransferases that methylate H3K4 and the MOF/NSL histone acetyltransferases that acetylate histone H4, as a direct interaction partner of MYC (Thomas et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thomas et al., 2015.

claim: MYC binds to WDR5 with a KD of 9.3 µM via MYC BoxIII.
source: MYC binds to WDR5 with a KD of 9.3 µM via MYC BoxIII (Thomas et al., 2015), a domain that is not part of the DNA-binding domain, suggesting that binding of MYC to WDR5 occurs independently of binding to DNA.
evidence: Supported by citation to Thomas et al., 2015.

claim: Binding of MYC to WDR5 occurs independently of binding to DNA.
source: MYC binds to WDR5 with a KD of 9.3 µM via MYC BoxIII (Thomas et al., 2015), a domain that is not part of the DNA-binding domain, suggesting that binding of MYC to WDR5 occurs independently of binding to DNA.
evidence: Based on the fact that MYC BoxIII is not part of the DNA-binding domain.

claim: The MYC/WDR5 interaction predicts an EC50 value of 0.014 µM for MYC occupancy of an E-box in the presence of WDR5.
source: A modified model (model 2; Figure 3F; see also Appendix 1) that assumes (i) that WDR5 is constantly bound to its target sites (ii) that MYC and WDR5 are free to bind to each other when both are bound to chromatin in close proximity predicts an EC50 value of 0.014 µM for MYC occupancy of an E-box in the presence of WDR5 (Figure 3G).
evidence: Based on mathematical modeling shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The MYC/WDR5 interaction is of sufficient high affinity to explain the high occupancy of promoters with low EC50 values (7,963/8,425).
source: This value is lower than the one estimated experimentally for the large majority of promoters, arguing that the MYC/WDR5 interaction is of sufficient high affinity to explain the high occupancy of promoters with low EC50 values (7,963/8,425).
evidence: Based on comparison of modeled and experimental EC50 values.

claim: The majority of promoters is bound by WDR5.
source: In agreement with the published data, our re-analysis showed that (i) the majority of promoters is bound by WDR5, (ii) almost all binding sites of MYC in promoters overlap with WDR5 binding and (iii) disruption of the interaction between MYC and WDR5 strongly decreases MYC binding to chromatin (Figure 4D).
evidence: Based on re-analysis of published ChIP-sequencing data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Almost all binding sites of MYC in promoters overlap with WDR5 binding.
source: In agreement with the published data, our re-analysis showed that (i) the majority of promoters is bound by WDR5, (ii) almost all binding sites of MYC in promoters overlap with WDR5 binding and (iii) disruption of the interaction between MYC and WDR5 strongly decreases MYC binding to chromatin (Figure 4D).
evidence: Based on re-analysis of published ChIP-sequencing data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Disruption of the interaction between MYC and WDR5 strongly decreases MYC binding to chromatin.
source: In agreement with the published data, our re-analysis showed that (i) the majority of promoters is bound by WDR5, (ii) almost all binding sites of MYC in promoters overlap with WDR5 binding and (iii) disruption of the interaction between MYC and WDR5 strongly decreases MYC binding to chromatin (Figure 4D).
evidence: Based on re-analysis of published ChIP-sequencing data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Eliminating MYC's ability to interact with WDR5 most strongly affects high-affinity binding sites with low EC50 values.
source: Strikingly, analysis of MYCWBM binding in HEK293 cells showed that eliminating MYC's ability to interact with WDR5 most strongly affects high-affinity binding sites with low EC50 values (Figure 4E).
evidence: Based on analysis of mutant MYC binding shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Known interactions of MYC with DNA together with promoter-bound factors can account for the range of promoter occupancies observed in vivo.
source: We conclude that known interactions of MYC with DNA together with promoter-bound factors can account for the range of promoter occupancies observed in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling and experimental data.

claim: There is a strong anti-correlation between the recruitment of exogenous MYC and the occurrence of E-boxes.
source: Importantly, we found a strong anti-correlation between the recruitment of exogenous MYC on one hand and the occurrence of E-boxes (Figure 4F), the expression level of target genes (Figure 4G) and trimethylation of histone H3K4 (Figure 4H) on the other hand.
evidence: Supported by binned plot analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: There is a strong anti-correlation between the recruitment of exogenous MYC and the expression level of target genes.
source: Importantly, we found a strong anti-correlation between the recruitment of exogenous MYC on one hand and the occurrence of E-boxes (Figure 4F), the expression level of target genes (Figure 4G) and trimethylation of histone H3K4 (Figure 4H) on the other hand.
evidence: Supported by binned plot analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: There is a strong anti-correlation between the recruitment of exogenous MYC and trimethylation of histone H3K4.
source: Importantly, we found a strong anti-correlation between the recruitment of exogenous MYC on one hand and the occurrence of E-boxes (Figure 4F), the expression level of target genes (Figure 4G) and trimethylation of histone H3K4 (Figure 4H) on the other hand.
evidence: Supported by binned plot analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The major change in occupancy is due to MYC binding to low-affinity binding sites and to weakly expressed genes when MYC levels increase.
source: This highlights that the major change in occupancy is due to MYC binding to low-affinity binding sites and to weakly expressed genes when MYC levels increase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the anti-correlation analysis.

claim: Genes encoding ribosomal proteins and proteins involved in ribosomal biogenesis are not regulated in response to doxycycline-mediated MYC overexpression.
source: Previously, we found that genes encoding ribosomal proteins and proteins involved in ribosomal biogenesis are not regulated in response to doxycycline-mediated MYC overexpression (Walz et al., 2014), supporting the hypothesis that MYC binding sites in their promoters are fully occupied by MYC at endogenous levels.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Walz et al., 2014).

claim: RNA-sequencing identified 753 genes being down-regulated and 1224 genes being significantly up-regulated upon siRNA-mediated depletion of MYC.
source: RNA-sequencing identified 753 genes being down- and 1224 genes being significantly up-regulated (log2FC < −1 or > 1, q-value < 0.01, Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Ribosomal protein genes and genes encoding proteins involved in ribosomal biogenesis are most strongly down-regulated upon siRNA-mediated depletion of MYC.
source: Strikingly, ribosomal protein genes and genes encoding proteins involved in ribosomal biogenesis are most strongly down-regulated upon siRNA treatment (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Genes with the highest affinity for MYC most strongly respond to depletion of endogenous MYC.
source: Strikingly, genes, which show the highest affinity for MYC, most strongly respond to depletion of endogenous MYC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Ribosomal protein genes are strongly induced when the pre-tumor condition is compared to control cells in the Eµ-MYC B cell lymphoma model.
source: Strikingly, ribosomal protein genes, hence the genes with lowest EC50 values, are strongly induced when the pre-tumor condition is compared to control cells (Figure 5F,H).
evidence: Based on re-analysis of published expression data shown in Figure 5F,H.

claim: Expression of ribosomal protein genes does not increase further when tumors are compared with pre-tumor cells in the Eµ-MYC model, although MYC protein levels increase about eight fold.
source: In contrast, expression of ribosomal protein genes does not increase further when tumors are compared with pre-tumor cells (Figure 5G,H), although MYC protein levels increase about eight fold (Sabò et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on re-analysis of published expression data shown in Figure 5G,H and citation to Sabò et al., 2014.

claim: Selective transcriptional responses by MYC at physiological and oncogenic levels are similar in vivo and in vitro.
source: Therefore, we propose that selective transcriptional responses by MYC at physiological and oncogenic levels are similar in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing U2OS cell data with the Eµ-MYC mouse model data.

claim: Gene sets that are strongly regulated upon MYC overexpression show a significantly higher median EC50 value than gene sets derived from the depletion of endogenous MYC.
source: Gene sets, which are strongly regulated upon overexpression, for example, genes involved in angiogenesis and cell migration (Figure 5I, orange boxplots), show a significantly higher median EC50 value than gene sets derived from the depletion of endogenous MYC (Figure 5I, blue boxplots).
evidence: Supported by boxplot analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Genes involved in circadian rhythm are regulated upon MYC overexpression and show high EC50 values.
source: We noted that also genes involved in circadian rhythm are regulated upon MYC overexpression and showed high EC50 values, consistent with the recent demonstration that disruption of the circadian clock is a critical transforming function of MYC (Altman et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on the authors' analysis and citation to Altman et al., 2015.

claim: Binding affinity determines specific MYC-mediated transcriptional responses at physiological and oncogenic MYC concentrations.
source: We concluded that binding affinity determines specific MYC-mediated transcriptional responses at physiological and oncogenic MYC concentrations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comprehensive analysis of EC50 values and gene regulation.

claim: EC50 values of genes that are down-regulated upon deletion of endogenous MYC in embryonic fibroblasts are very low.
source: Strikingly, EC50 values of genes that are down-regulated upon deletion of endogenous MYC are very low (Figure 5I, green boxplot) confirming that, as in U2OS cells, at physiological levels MYC regulates genes with the highest binding affinity.
evidence: Based on analysis of published expression data from mouse embryonic fibroblasts shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Promoters of genes encoding proteins involved in lipid metabolism, purine metabolism, and potentially glycolysis show elevated EC50 values.
source: In view of reports, which demonstrate that altering cellular metabolism is a transforming mechanism of MYC (Stine et al., 2015), we analyzed the affinity of promoters of genes encoding proteins involved in selected metabolic processes and indeed observed elevated EC50 values for lipid- and purine metabolism and potentially glycolysis (Figure 5I, violet boxplots).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 5I and citation to Stine et al., 2015.

claim: MYC regulates different sets of genes at physiological and oncogenic levels.
source: Our data suggest that MYC regulates different sets of genes at physiological and oncogenic levels and that these gene sets can be stratified by promoter affinity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comprehensive analysis of MYC levels and gene regulation.

claim: Different gene sets can be stratified by promoter affinity for MYC.
source: Our data suggest that MYC regulates different sets of genes at physiological and oncogenic levels and that these gene sets can be stratified by promoter affinity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EC50 analysis and gene set enrichment studies.

claim: Analysis of gene expression profiles at five different concentrations of doxycycline revealed different response patterns for different gene sets.
source: Analysis of gene expression profiles at five different concentrations of doxycycline revealed different response patterns for different gene sets (Figure 6B), ranging from hardly any response to MYC overexpression ('structural constituent of ribosome'), medium-level responses ('ribonucleoprotein complex biogenesis'), to gene sets, which responded predominantly at very high MYC levels ('substrate-specific transporter activity').
evidence: Supported by heat map analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The observed differences in dose response correlate with the promoter affinity of the genes involved in these processes.
source: The RNA-sequencing data enabled us to calculate EC50 values for regulation and to correlate them with EC50 values for binding. Importantly, the observed differences in dose response correlate with the promoter affinity of the genes involved in these processes (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Differences in promoter affinity can account for the distinct transcriptional response programs observed in biological systems exhibiting different MYC expression levels.
source: We conclude that differences in promoter affinity can account for the distinct transcriptional response programs observed in biological systems exhibiting different MYC expression levels (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comprehensive analysis of MYC levels, promoter affinity, and gene regulation.

claim: Direct MYC-mediated repression is most apparent at high levels of MYC.
source: As direct repression is most apparent at high levels of MYC (Wiese et al., 2015), we hypothesized that differences in MYC expression levels might explain this seeming contradiction.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wiese et al., 2015.

claim: Direct MYC-mediated repression largely depends on complex formation with MIZ1.
source: Direct MYC-mediated repression largely depends on complex formation with MIZ1 (Peukert et al., 1997), which is strongly reduced when expressing a point mutant of MYC (MYCV394D).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peukert et al., 1997.

claim: MYC/MIZ1-mediated repression takes place at high levels of MYC.
source: Interestingly MYC/MIZ1-mediated repression takes place at high levels of MYC, both in a global analysis (Figure 6D) as well as for individual genes (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by heat map and qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Genes directly repressed by MYC show significantly higher EC50 values than transactivated genes.
source: Accordingly, genes directly repressed by MYC ('Down (direct)' in Figure 6F), show significantly higher EC50 values than transactivated genes ('Up'), whereas indirectly repressed genes ('Down (indirect)' in Figure 6F) show affinities comparable to that of transactivated genes.
evidence: Supported by boxplot analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Indirectly repressed genes show affinities comparable to that of transactivated genes.
source: Accordingly, genes directly repressed by MYC ('Down (direct)' in Figure 6F), show significantly higher EC50 values than transactivated genes ('Up'), whereas indirectly repressed genes ('Down (indirect)' in Figure 6F) show affinities comparable to that of transactivated genes.
evidence: Supported by boxplot analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Direct MYC-mediated repression is a predominant form of transcriptional regulation at high (oncogenic) levels of MYC.
source: We concluded that direct MYC-mediated repression is a predominant form of transcriptional regulation at high (oncogenic) levels of MYC, which may not be reached during normal cell growth (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of MYC/MIZ1-mediated repression.

claim: Direct interaction with DNA alone is not sufficient to account for the observed occupancies of core promoters by MYC/MAX complexes.
source: The first conclusion is that direct interaction with DNA alone is not sufficient to account for the observed occupancies of core promoters by MYC/MAX complexes.
evidence: This is a major conclusion from the mathematical modeling and experimental data.

claim: The positions occupied by MYC/MAX complexes across the human genome closely correlate with the RNA polymerase II transcription machinery even on promoters which do not contain E-boxes.
source: This result is in agreement with experimental observations showing that the positions occupied by MYC/MAX complexes across the human genome closely correlate with the RNA polymerase II transcription machinery even on promoters, which do not contain E-boxes (Guccione et al., 2006; Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guccione et al., 2006 and Guo et al., 2014.

claim: The interaction of MYC/MAX with promoter-bound WDR5 can strongly enhance occupancy of core promoters.
source: The mathematical analysis shows that the interaction of MYC/MAX with promoter-bound WDR5 can strongly enhance occupancy of core promoters.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical modeling shown in the manuscript.

claim: A mutant allele of MYC unable to bind to WDR5 shows much reduced binding to high-affinity promoters.
source: Consistent with this finding, a mutant allele of MYC unable to bind to WDR5 shows much reduced binding to high-affinity promoters.
evidence: Based on re-analysis of published ChIP-sequencing data for mutant MYC.

claim: MYC interacts with several components of the transcription machinery including P-TEFb, TBP and TRRAP.
source: MYC does not only interact with WDR5, but with several components of the transcription machinery including P-TEFb, TBP and TRRAP (Bouchard et al., 2004; Eberhardy and Farnham, 2002; Hateboer et al., 1993; McMahon et al., 1998; Rahl et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple publications.

claim: MYC BoxI interacts with the PAF1C complex that is located at core promoters.
source: Additionally, we recently identified the interaction of another conserved domain of MYC, MYC BoxI, with the PAF1C complex that is located at core promoters (Jaenicke et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jaenicke et al., 2016.

claim: Genome-wide occupancies of MYC/MAX complexes result both from interactions of MYC/MAX complexes with DNA and from protein/protein interactions with resident chromatin proteins.
source: Most likely, therefore, genome-wide occupancies of MYC/MAX complexes result both from interactions of MYC/MAX complexes with DNA and from protein/protein interactions with resident chromatin proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comprehensive analysis of MYC binding.

claim: The dependence of MYC/MAX chromatin binding on interactions with proteins that are themselves influenced by existing gene expression patterns contributes to specific gene regulation by MYC.
source: We propose that the dependence of MYC/MAX chromatin binding on interactions with proteins that are themselves influenced by existing gene expression patterns at different physiological states of cells, contributes to specific gene regulation by MYC even though MYC´s mechanism of action is the same at all promoters (as an example, see Liu et al. (2015)).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings, with citation to Liu et al., 2015.

claim: Conserved protein/protein interactions of MYC are critical for targeting MYC/MAX complexes to specific classes of binding sites such as core promoters in vivo.
source: Our analysis leads to the hypothesis that conserved protein/protein interactions of MYC are critical for targeting MYC/MAX complexes to specific classes of binding sites such as core promoters in vivo.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their analysis.

claim: Promoter affinity for MYC confers specificity to gene regulation.
source: The second conclusion that can be drawn from our data is that promoter affinity for MYC confers specificity to gene regulation.
evidence: This is a major conclusion from the comprehensive analysis of promoter affinity and gene regulation.

claim: There is a close correlation between apparent promoter affinity measured by ChIP-sequencing and response to different concentrations of MYC measured by RNA-sequencing.
source: Our results show that promoters differ in their apparent affinity for MYC and demonstrate a close correlation between apparent promoter affinity measured by ChIP-sequencing and response to different concentrations of MYC measured by RNA-sequencing at different MYC levels.
evidence: Based on the correlation analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: A gene is regulated by MYC in a given experimental setting if the occupancy of its promoter (or a relevant enhancer) by MYC changes in this setting.
source: This correlation leads to the conclusion that a gene is regulated by MYC in a given experimental setting, if the occupancy of its promoter (or a relevant enhancer) by MYC changes in this setting.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between promoter occupancy and gene regulation.

claim: Promoters can be saturated by levels of MYC that are reached in proliferating cells.
source: Importantly, measurements of MYC levels and modeling approaches show that promoters can be saturated by levels of MYC that are reached in proliferating cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: Based on MYC quantification and mathematical modeling.

claim: Expression of genes may not respond to MYC in a certain experimental setting since the promoters are fully occupied before addition of doxycycline.
source: As a result, expression of genes may not respond to MYC in a certain experimental setting (such as a doxycycline-mediated induction of high MYC levels) since the promoters are fully occupied before addition of doxycycline.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed lack of response of certain genes to MYC overexpression.

claim: Strongly transcribed genes such as many ribosomal protein genes and genes encoding proteins involved in ribosome biogenesis and translation are likely to have promoters fully occupied before addition of doxycycline.
source: This is likely to be true for strongly transcribed genes as many ribosomal protein genes and genes encoding proteins involved in ribosome biogenesis and translation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed saturation of high-affinity promoters.

claim: The experimentally observed specificity in gene regulation can be explained without the need to invoke productive and non-productive modes of interaction of MYC with chromatin.
source: The experimentally observed specificity in gene regulation can therefore be explained without the need to invoke productive and non-productive modes of interaction of MYC with chromatin.
evidence: This is a conclusion that reconciles the two conflicting models of MYC function.

claim: MYC can contribute to oncogenic transformation via two different mechanisms: low levels of constitutive MYC enhance expression of genes with high-affinity promoters, and additional increases in MYC levels enhance occupancy of promoters that are lowly occupied in normal and proliferating cells.
source: Consistent with this notion, the analysis of MYC-driven lymphomagenesis shows that MYC can contribute to oncogenic transformation via two different mechanisms: low levels of constitutive MYC enhance expression of genes with high-affinity promoters, such as genes encoding proteins involved in ribosome function. This is seen when pre-tumorigenic B-cells are compared with control lymphocytes. MYC levels further increase at the transition to frank lymphomas and there is clear evidence for further increases in MYC levels during progression of several tumor entities, as for example in APC-mutant colorectal tumors (Kress et al., 2011; Myant and Sansom, 2011; Siemens et al., 2011). This additional increase in MYC levels will enhance occupancy of promoters that are lowly occupied in normal and proliferating cells.
evidence: Based on analysis of the Eµ-MYC lymphoma model and citations to studies on tumor progression.

claim: There is clear evidence for further increases in MYC levels during progression of several tumor entities, as for example in APC-mutant colorectal tumors.
source: MYC levels further increase at the transition to frank lymphomas and there is clear evidence for further increases in MYC levels during progression of several tumor entities, as for example in APC-mutant colorectal tumors (Kress et al., 2011; Myant and Sansom, 2011; Siemens et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kress et al., 2011; Myant and Sansom, 2011; Siemens et al., 2011.

claim: Additional increases in MYC levels will alter the physiological and metabolic state of the tumor cells.
source: Since differences in apparent affinity and in EC50 values stratify classes of promoters of genes that encode proteins that differ in function, we propose that this will alter the physiological and metabolic state (Stine et al., 2015) of the tumor cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a proposal based on the authors' findings, with citation to Stine et al., 2015.

claim: Promoters with the lowest apparent affinity are found in genes that encode proteins involved in nutrient transport, G-protein coupled receptors and in the response to hypoxia.
source: Notably, promoters with the lowest apparent affinity are found in genes that encode proteins involved in nutrient transport, G-protein coupled receptors and in the response to hypoxia.
evidence: Based on the gene set enrichment analysis of EC50 values.

claim: Expression of genes encoding proteins involved in nutrient transport, G-protein coupled receptors and response to hypoxia responds to further increases in MYC levels.
source: Expression of these genes responds to further increases in MYC levels arguing that they are the basis for the selective pressure for increases in MYC levels.
evidence: Based on the dose-response analysis of gene expression at different MYC levels.

claim: Many tumors depend on ('are addicted to') high MYC levels.
source: Since many tumors depend on ('are addicted to') high MYC levels, inhibition of proteins encoded by this class of target genes can be a rational strategy for selective inhibition of MYC-dependent tumor growth.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about MYC addiction in tumors.

claim: Inhibition of proteins encoded by low-affinity MYC target genes can be a rational strategy for selective inhibition of MYC-dependent tumor growth.
source: Since many tumors depend on ('are addicted to') high MYC levels, inhibition of proteins encoded by this class of target genes can be a rational strategy for selective inhibition of MYC-dependent tumor growth.
evidence: This is a therapeutic hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Virtually all genes that are repressed by MYC/MAX in complex with MIZ1 display low apparent affinities and high EC50 values.
source: Finally, we note that virtually all genes that are repressed by MYC/MAX in complex with MIZ1 display low apparent affinities and high EC50 values, suggesting that MIZ1-mediated repression occurs predominantly at high MYC levels.
evidence: Based on the analysis of EC50 values for MYC/MIZ1-repressed genes.

claim: MIZ1-mediated repression occurs predominantly at high MYC levels.
source: Finally, we note that virtually all genes that are repressed by MYC/MAX in complex with MIZ1 display low apparent affinities and high EC50 values, suggesting that MIZ1-mediated repression occurs predominantly at high MYC levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the EC50 analysis of MYC/MIZ1-repressed genes.

claim: MIZ1-mediated repression is required for tumor formation in MYC-driven lymphoma.
source: MIZ1-mediated repression is required for tumor formation in MYC-driven lymphoma (van Riggelen et al., 2010) and medulloblastoma (Vo et al., 2016), suggesting that targeting the complex may provide a second strategy with a significant therapeutic window for MYC-dependent tumors.
evidence: Supported by citations to van Riggelen et al., 2010 and Vo et al., 2016.

claim: MIZ1-mediated repression is required for tumor formation in MYC-driven medulloblastoma.
source: MIZ1-mediated repression is required for tumor formation in MYC-driven lymphoma (van Riggelen et al., 2010) and medulloblastoma (Vo et al., 2016), suggesting that targeting the complex may provide a second strategy with a significant therapeutic window for MYC-dependent tumors.
evidence: Supported by citations to van Riggelen et al., 2010 and Vo et al., 2016.

claim: Targeting the MYC/MIZ1 complex may provide a strategy with a significant therapeutic window for MYC-dependent tumors.
source: MIZ1-mediated repression is required for tumor formation in MYC-driven lymphoma (van Riggelen et al., 2010) and medulloblastoma (Vo et al., 2016), suggesting that targeting the complex may provide a second strategy with a significant therapeutic window for MYC-dependent tumors.
evidence: This is a therapeutic hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the requirement of MIZ1 for tumor formation.

claim: Doxycycline-induced overexpression of MYC in U2OS cells establishes a gene expression signature which closely resembles multiple established signatures of MYC target genes.
source: We showed previously that doxycycline-induced overexpression of MYC in these cells establishes a gene expression signature, which closely resembles multiple established signatures of MYC target genes and identifies expression signatures of patients with MYC amplification in tumors (Walz et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Walz et al., 2014).

claim: Doxycycline-induced overexpression of MYC in U2OS cells identifies expression signatures of patients with MYC amplification in tumors.
source: We showed previously that doxycycline-induced overexpression of MYC in these cells establishes a gene expression signature, which closely resembles multiple established signatures of MYC target genes and identifies expression signatures of patients with MYC amplification in tumors (Walz et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Walz et al., 2014).
